utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I repeat the suggestion earlier on, though, that if communications are to be made from the Prosecution, the ultimate purpose of which is to communicate with the witness, then they ought to be communications which are shared with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will communicate to the Defence whatever I've said to Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Karnavas can communicate it back to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. No. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What we don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It goes more directly, Mr. Re. If there's anything you would like to bring to the attention of Mr. Karnavas and that is indirectly -- to the attention of Mr. Davidson under those circumstances, of course, the communication between Mr. Kabashi and Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Davidson is privileged. But if you want to bring something to the attention of Mr. Karnavas and where you offer that you would tell everything to the Defence, then let them be present so that they can hear immediately what is communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, we're losing time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I understand that. And that's why -- there's a point here. Mr. Davidson said and has said a number of times he does not want -- that Kabashi does not want to testify today. What does "today" mean? Until you actually -- until someone speaks to him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Bring this to the attention of Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Davidson. And as far as Mr. Kabashi is included, I think you should be excluded. And if you just speak to Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Davidson on these matters, then the Defence -- where you offered to tell them in its entirety what you discussed with Mr. Karnavas, the most direct way of informing them about it is that they are present.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm very happy to speak to Mr. Karnavas and then as soon as I speak to them go straight to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the two of us say what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, this is not a debating club. This is a court of law in which the Chamber has ruled on the communications, which may take the 15 minutes from now on. If you want to speak with Mr. Karnavas about these matters, then take care and perhaps also, Defence counsel, to the extent they want to attend, take care that someone else to hear a few other decisions the Chamber will deliver during these 15 minutes. Therefore, I -- everyone who wants to leave the courtroom at this moment is excused. We will suspend the videolink for 15 minutes. We'll continue the hearing in The Hague. If there are any communications at this moment, Mr. -- Let me just see. Mr. Davidson and Mr. Karnavas, you -- you are, of course -- it goes without saying. You're free to communicate with Mr. Kabashi however -- however, Mr. Re can communicate with Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Davidson, not directly with Mr. Kabashi. Mr. Troop -- let's first finish this. Is this understood? And Mr. Tarlow -- I -- this Chamber ruled on ways of communication. If there's anything you would like to bring to our attention because it might be relevant under your domestic law, you have an opportunity to do so. If not, we'll just suspend the videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. TARLOW
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I think I just want to make sure that I understand where things stand. It's my understanding that Mr. Davidson and Mr. Karnavas may now speak to Mr. Re but it must also be in the presence of Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the situation. And, of course, Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Davidson can speak to each other as they wish, even if -- even if Mr. Kabashi, of course, would be present or would listen to it -- their conversation or even participate in their conversation. But whenever the Prosecution in The Hague is involved in such a conversation, it should be in the absence of Mr. Kabashi and in the presence of the -- The Hague Defence. UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: Okay. But certainly there's nothing to prevent Mr. Kabashi from speaking with Mr. Davidson and/or Mr. Karnavas in privacy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's no objection against that in whatever way. I take it that he would then receive advice on his present legal situation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No objection. I'm here. I'll wait for a call from anyone who wants to call me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It will not be me, Mr. Davidson, but -- as you will understand. We suspend the videolink for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop, let me just try to imagine what your problem is, that you're alone today. Not -- I can indicate that the Chamber intends to deliver a decision on, could I say, the interrupted 92 quater decision now considering additional information the Chamber has received, where under normal circumstances one would wait until an English translation of a German document is available, the Chamber considers under the present circumstances that there's no need to wait for that. Then the second decision the Chamber intends to deliver is about -- may I say the three 92 bis statements against the one new 92 bis statement. That's a decision, of course -- and the third one is about the reasons for an extension of time in order to -- the Kabashi decision which already has been delivered, but the reasons still to be given. And also including a decision on the Prosecution's motion to hear Witness 30 via videolink. But the Chamber will refrain from any further discussions at this moment and we'll just deliver these decisions. If you would like to have a written, although non-authoritative statement, of course, you could look at the -- at your screen later on. But if you would prefer to have something to read on paper, then there might be a solution for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm content to read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Subsequently, simply for formal reasons, perhaps I could ask Ms. Antoniette Trapani, my legal assistant who's present in court, to represent my client's interests during my absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, is she qualified to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: She's -- she's not formally qualified, but she can certainly get my attention if -- if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: -- if anything arises which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If anything arises which bothers her -- then whenever she then leaves the courtroom, we'll make a pause in order to take care that Mr. Brahimaj is not unrepresented. If that's an agreeable solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I don't know who is going to leave or not to leave the courtroom for making telephone calls. I leave it entirely to everyone. Although, I would be a bit surprised if no one leaves the courtroom to make phone calls. Meanwhile, the Chamber will deliver --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It looks like we are all going to stay here so we can all hear the decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm not -- I take it that Mr. Re would -- would like to speak to Mr. Karnavas under the present circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll leave Ms. Schweiger here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it looks like an exodus but ... Then the Chamber will deliver first the decision on the Prosecution's motion to admit evidence under Rule 92 quater. It is the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's motion to admit evidence under Rule 92 quater as filed on the 5th of November, 2007. The Prosecution's motion concerns one of the witnesses who was added to the Prosecution's witness list following the Chamber's decision to amend the indictment on the 15th of October, 2007. On the 16th of October, the Prosecution sought to have the statement of this witness admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. When the Registry's presiding officer attempted to obtain the necessary attestation, the witness refused. According to the Prosecution's motion, the witness stated on this occasion that he did not want to sign anything and that he would not go to The Hague unless he was forced to do so. The Prosecution has based its Rule 92 quater application on the witness's medical condition and the fact that the witness is of advanced age. The medical certificate accompanying the Prosecution's motion indicates that the witness suffers from physical and mental ailments, without further specifics, and that the witness has been under continuous medical treatment since 1999. The Defence for the three accused responded on the 8th, the 13th, and the 14th of November that the Prosecution's motion should be denied. On the 20th of November, the Prosecution submitted an additional medical certificate providing further details about the witness's health condition. The Chamber observes that the medical certificates do not satisfy the Chamber that the witness is unable by reason of bodily conditions to testify orally in this case. Moreover, the witness appears to have told the Registry's presiding officer, or I should say the presiding officer appointed by the Registrar, that he was unwilling, rather than unable, to give testimony in The Hague or to attest to the statement he previously had given to the Prosecution. The Chamber has also considered that the additional medical certificate refers to a condition of chronic post-traumatic shock - at least, that's how it reads in German, "schock" - I take it that the Prosecution is so familiar with the German language so as to -- to correct me if I wrongly translate the word "schock" into "shock" in English. So a condition of chronic post-traumatic shock and pre-senile dementia. To the extent this demonstrates a mental condition which disenables the witness to testify, it also immediately raises the issue - given the fact that the statement was taken in 2003 - of -- the issue of the chronic character of the post-traumatic shock and how long the witness has suffered from pre-senile dementia. These are circumstances the Chamber has to consider under Rule 92 quater (A)(ii) in view of the effect they may have on the reliability of the statement. Taken together, the Chamber is not satisfied that the written statement meets the requirements in Rule 92 quater for admission. And the Chamber therefore denies the Prosecution's motion. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I now move to the decision on the Prosecution's submission of the statement of Witness 51 and the application for trial-related protective measures for this witness. On the 2nd of November, 2007, the Chamber admitted three statements of Witness 51, conditional upon receiving an attestation under Rule 92 bis (B) by the 15th of November, 2007. The Prosecution has not provided this attestation, so this conditional admission is now void. On the 13th of November, 2007, the Prosecution tendered a new statement of Witness 51 dated the 8th of November, 2007, with an attestation under Rule 92 bis (B). Compared with the previous conditionally admitted statements, paragraph 14 and 16 are entirely new and paragraph 15 contains some new information. On the 19th of November, 2007, the Defence for Mr. Haradinaj and Mr. -- for Mr. Balaj filed separate submissions on the matter, objecting to the admission into evidence of the new statement of Witness 51. On the 19th of November, 2007, the Defence for Mr. Brahimaj joined in the submissions of the Defence for Mr. Haradinaj. On the 20th of November, 2007, the Prosecution filed its reply to the Defence submissions on the matter, seeking leave to reply to the Defence responses and guidance as to whether it should seek Rule 92 bis (B) attestations for the three conditionally admitted statements of Witness 51. Concerning the admissibility of the statement under Rule 92 bis, the Chamber refers to its decision of the 2nd of November, 2007. The Chamber considers that the new information contained in paragraphs 14 through 16 does not warrant a different approach. On the 13th of November, 2007, the Prosecution requested that Witness 51 be allowed to retain her pseudonym and that a redacted version of her statement be admitted into evidence. The legal test for granting protective measures applied by this Chamber has been set forth numerous times and there is no need to repeat it. The Prosecution reported that no threats have been made against Witness 51. The witness owns property in Kosovo, and the witness's statement describes the identification of the remains of missing relatives and the attempts at exhumation of the graves of these missing relatives. The Chamber cannot see how this evidence may antagonise people who reside in Kosovo. Therefore, the Chamber denies the Prosecution's application for trial-related protective measures. The Chamber admits the new 92 bis statement of Witness 51 into evidence. The Chamber instructs the Prosecution to upload the 92 bis witness statement of Witness 51 into e-court and instructs the Registrar to assign an exhibit number to it and inform the Chamber and parties of the exhibit number so assigned. The Chamber orders the Registrar to make public the evidence of Witness 51, unless the Prosecution informs the Chamber and the Registrar by 5.00 p.m. on the 22nd of November, 2007 that it prefers to withdraw the witness's evidence. The Chamber grants the Prosecution's request for leave to reply to the Defence's responses and instructs the Prosecution not to seek Rule 92 bis (B) attestations for the three previous conditionally admitted statements of Witness 51. And this concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter. I now move on to the reasons for granting an extension of time in order to hear Kabashi's testimony and a decision on Prosecution's motion to hear Witness 30 via videolink. The Chamber would now like to address these two issues in relation to the extensions of the Prosecution's case. Firstly, with regard to today's witness, the parties will recall that on the 1st of November, 2007, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's motion to hear Mr. Kabashi's evidence via videolink. On the 14th of November, 2007, the Prosecution filed a motion requesting that the evidence of Mr. Kabashi be heard on the 20th of November. On the 15th of November, 2007, the Chamber granted this request, stating that it would give the reasons for this decision in due course. In taking this decision, the Chamber was mindful of the fact that on the 31st of October, 2007 it announced that it expected the Prosecution to close its case on the 16th of November, 2007. However, the Prosecution has shown that it exhausted all reasonable efforts to secure the evidence of Mr. Kabashi by this date, and due to circumstances out of the Prosecution's control, this was not possible. The Chamber therefore decided to grant the Prosecution's -- to grant the Prosecution an extension of time to complete its case for the sole purpose of hearing Mr. Kabashi's evidence on the 20th of November, 2007. Secondly, having read -- having now read the submissions by the Defence, the Chamber would like to deliver its decision on whether to grant the Prosecution a further extension of time in order to hear the testimony of Witness 30. As the parties are aware, the Chamber is currently seized of an application by the Prosecution, filed on the 16th of November, 2007, for an extension of time in order to hear the testimony of Witness 30 on the 21st of November, 2007. As with the previously mentioned witness, the Prosecution argue that it exhausted all reasonable efforts to secure the evidence of Witness 30 by the 16th of November but it was unable to do so for reasons beyond its control. The Defence responded in writing today, 20 November, arguing that the Prosecution has had ample time to make the necessary arrangements and with due diligence could have ensured his testimony before the end of its case. As such, the Defence submits that the Prosecution should not be granted a further extension to hear the testimony of Witness 30. The Chamber does not agree. The procedural history as depicted by the Defence does not adequately reflect the ongoing struggle to obtain Witness 30's evidence. Even if the momentum may have been lost for a short while, this is of minor import when balancing the expected importance of the evidence of Witness 30 for the OTP case against the difficulties the OTP faced in obtaining his testimony. The Chamber therefore grants the Prosecution's motion for an extension of time in order to hear the testimony of Witness 30. Further, due to the unavailability this week of lead counsel for Mr. Brahimaj for reasons that the Chamber finds understandable, the Prosecution is invited to call Witness 30 on the 26th and the 27th of November of this year. In issuing the decision, the Chamber would like to inform the Prosecution that this further extension of its case is of an exceptional nature and is granted for the sole purpose of hearing the evidence of Witness 30. For all other purposes, the Chamber regards the Prosecution's case as closed and hereby informs the Prosecution that it cannot use this extra time for the submission of any evidence not directly related to the scheduled testimony of Witness 30. And this completes -- concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter. Mr. Registrar, if I am not mistaken, since we interrupted the videolink, some 17 or 18 minutes have elapsed. Therefore, the Chamber would like to continue with the videolink, but we'll take one or two minutes to allow Mr. Re, Mr. Guy-Smith, Mr. Dixon, and Mr. Troop to return into the courtroom. I take it that those who are closest to the gentlemen I just mentioned are in a position to get them back into court within the next three or four minutes. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure what practical arrangements were made immediately after they left the room. That's the only reason why I hesitate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't know where they are, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, investigative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Upon further consideration, the Chamber, in awareness that five or six minutes would not do if we wanted to continue until 7.00, the Chamber decided that we'll have a break for 20 minutes, as usual. We'll resume at three minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just verify that the videolink is functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, we could hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kabashi, before we would continue, let's try to cut matters short. Although you may be well aware of it, Rule 77 tells you that being a witness before a Chamber, a contumacious refusal or failure to answer a question is considered to be contempt and the maximum penalty that may be imposed on a person who is found to be in contempt of the Tribunal is a term of imprisonment not exceeding seven years or a fine not exceeding 100.000 Euros, or both. Mr. Kabashi, before we adjourned, a question was put to you by Mr. Re which you failed to answer. And from your responses, I understood that you would not only not answer this question but you would not answer any question that would be put to you as a witness in the case in which you are now called to testify as a witness. Could you confirm that I understood this well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'm addressing Mr. -- you, Mr. Davidson and Mr. Karnavas. May I take it that you have advised Mr. Kabashi about his duty to testify and about his present position? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: [Via videolink] My advice to my client is -- is confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not asking for the advice. I'm asking whether you informed him about his position so that he is -- that whatever you advised him to do, whatever decision he takes, that he's well informed about the position he is in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I -- he's as well informed as I can make him. I -- I have to emphasise, I'm an American attorney. I have been assigned to this case for less than 24 hours and I've had very little opportunity to investigate the interplay between the laws and rules of your jurisdiction and American law, so frankly, I -- I cannot say that I can advise him fully about what consequences may actually flow from -- from a refusal to testify or failure to testify. I -- in an effort to cut this short, I can tell the Court, with all due respect, and after talking to Mr. Kabashi, that Mr. Kabashi is not going to testify today. I do not close the door on a modification of that position in the future, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: [Via videolink] And, again, I -- on this end, in terms of -- of the actual ramifications of any action that the International Court takes, I'm, frankly, not in a position to fully advise Mr. Kabashi today, because I -- this is very far outside my expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I did have a conversation out in the hallway with the Prosecutor -- or members of the Prosecution and with the Defence teams. The Prosecution informed me of the various consequences, how they saw them. I had a conversation with both the lawyer and Mr. Kabashi. I've informed Mr. Kabashi what I believe to be the various options that are available to him. I've informed him to the best of my ability, and I believe that Mr. Kabashi was listening very carefully and -- you know, at the end of the day, it's up to him to decide how and -- and what manner he wishes to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. And I'm -- I'm not seeking to be informed about any advice given, of course. It would be inappropriate to even ask for that. Then since it has been mentioned several times this afternoon that Mr. Kabashi will not testify today and where it's kept open as an option that that might be different on any -- any future day, apart from all the practicalities, I would just like to stress that a failure to answer a question is not undone by answering that question tomorrow or a week after that. I just want you, Mr. Kabashi, to know that it's not a kind of a mechanism that if I don't answer the question today but I do it tomorrow, that the failure to answer the question today could not be contemptuous any more. I just want you to know that. Is there -- I'm looking to the parties. Is there anything else we need to address at this moment? Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That -- that issue of Mr. -- where Mr. Davidson said a moment ago, Mr. -- after talking to Mr. Kabashi, "Mr. Kabashi is not going to testify today. I do not close the door on a modification of that position in the future." That -- that's what the Prosecution is very anxious to explore with Mr. Davidson or Mr. Karnavas, of course, with the Trial Chamber, as to what is meant by that. If Mr. Kabashi will, after receiving proper advice from his lawyer in the States, who has just frankly and candidly told the Trial Chamber that he's unaware and cannot properly advise his client, having just received the brief, so to speak, if Mr. Kabashi is in a position to change his mind later today, after he speaks to his lawyer, and maybe testify tomorrow. That's all we're very much interested in. Is that door open that Mr. Kabashi would reconsider and testify tomorrow, and then we could maybe move the proceedings forward. If Mr. Davidson could be asked that and maybe to communicate that, we might be able to resolve this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, it's -- it's not a legal expression to say "never say never," but it might come close to that. We have now struggled with these -- this issue for many, many months. If a dramatic change -- and I think it needs more to say perhaps not today, perhaps tomorrow, that's not a dramatic change. If -- if there would be dramatic changes and if Mr. Kabashi, for whom we, I think, once lifted the execution of an arrest warrant because he indicated that -- that he would come to The Hague and to testify, and that to have -- we had to reinstate that -- the execution of the arrest warrant soon after that, because Mr. Kabashi's intentions were not the same as his behaviour. You know where we are, that is, at the very, very end of the Prosecution's case. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now to anticipate what the Chamber would do if suddenly matters would be entirely different, I think the Chamber will just wait and see what happens. And the Chamber is aware and takes it that you're aware as well that it's one minute to 12.00. That means there are 60 seconds left until 12.00 and that there is still something on our agenda until 12.00. But if there would be dramatic changes, the Chamber will hear of them. At the same time, the Chamber will not engage in an endless continuing story. That should be clear. And, of course, the Chamber is not in a position to -- to in any way be an obstacle to whatever you would like to initiate, but you should not expect that every expectation of further testimony will be followed by permission of the Chamber to follow that course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not -- I -- my submission is we're not asking for a great deal at this particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber -- the Chamber waits --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We're just asking for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber waits and sees what you come up with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just asking for the door to be left ajar. We have the Registry officer in the United States at the moment receiving the testimony. We have Mr. Kabashi being advised competently by a public defender, a senior public defender who says he needs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But are you talking about today or tomorrow or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, the -- his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean -- I mean, we had -- we --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just -- I just said -- I just said a moment ago if we could explore with his lawyer what he means by "today". Because his lawyer has just said in the States --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But please, Mr. -- Mr. -- Mr. Re, do so in court. You know there are exactly 35 minutes which would be available anyhow for interpreters, technicians, et cetera. I've not even invited them to stay on stand-by. We spent approximately one hour previously -- or at least, we gave an opportunity for approximately one hour to further discuss these matters. And I do understand that what you would like us to decide is that everyone should remain stand-by until 7.00. Is that ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's a start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, a start.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I -- can I please address you on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For the first time Mr.-- as far as I know, Mr. Kabashi has a lawyer with him in the States who is advising him competently on his rights and the issues and what may or may not occur in the future in relation to his decision. It would appear, based upon what his lawyer has just said to the Trial Chamber, that his lawyer has not been able to inform him of everything, because his lawyer is not fully aware of all the consequences of the decision which Mr. Kabashi may or may not make. That is because his lawyer just said he's not aware of the interplay between the United States jurisdiction and the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. It may be, if the lawyer can speak to his client today, become more apprised of the situation without my assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It may be -- and the -- and the videolink is -- is there. The Registry is there. Everything has been put in place. That if he receives advice based upon -- fully informed advice based upon a full appreciation of the powers of this Tribunal and the consequences of failing to testify and the continuing contempt, or in my submission, another contempt has been committed today, and the consequences of that, he may change his mind. And if we leave it until a bit later to see whether he would, leave it till today, and maybe -- maybe, overnight, there's one more chance. And the Prosecution just asks the Trial Chamber, given we're at this position now, one minute to midnight, to give us that extra possibility to have this important evidence heard. And not to give up at this particular point. That's all we're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: [Via videolink] May I be heard?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- the interpreters note that the witness said, we think -- we are not 100 per cent sure. He said that, "I didn't say -- I never said I would not come to testify." Maybe he -- you should ask him again to confirm his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I -- it is on the -- on our screen that Mr. Davidson asked to be heard on the matter. Mr. Davidson, you have an opportunity to -- to say what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I simply -- thank you, Your Honour. I simply want to say I don't think it's realistic to think that there's going to be any change in position in the next hour or even in the next 24 hours. I have yet to have an opportunity to speak at length with my client with the assistance of an interpreter. I emphasise again I understand what I have been told by the Prosecutors over there with -- with regard to the -- the consequences for this witness if -- if he doesn't testify. What I don't know has to do with -- with, you know, what the -- what the actual practical effect of that would be. I also have had no opportunity, I should say on the record, to investigate whether there may be any privileges that he's in a position to assert with -- with regard to the subject matter of his testimony. You know, once again, I understand that extensive logistical arrangements have been made for this proceeding today. I will say I was not privy to any of those arrangements, and I first encountered this defendant, once again, yesterday afternoon. In any event, I do not want to mislead the Court by -- by suggesting that with another hour, if you stay up late or something like that, that that's going to change anything. I will also tell the Court we are on the verge of a major holiday weekend here in the United States. This court is going to be closed on Thursday and Friday. I believe it is going to close early tomorrow. So -- so for us to -- for me to do anything further productively with this defendant is -- is going to take well into next week. And I -- I simply don't think you should be concerned with -- with sitting for another hour today, because I don't think that there's anything productive that I could do that I haven't done already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Defence here in The Hague. Anything to be added?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Not at this stage, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith. Nodding "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Nothing at this time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We read on the screen that -- Mr. Kabashi, that you wanted to say something we may not have heard. You have an opportunity to repeat what you said or to say something. At the same time, I'm not expecting you to explain why you don't want to give testimony, because that's an issue which has been sufficiently dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I -- I'm good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The defendant -- or, I'm sorry, the witness does not wish to say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- Mr. Kabashi, you heard Mr. Davidson saying that it would be unrealistically to expect any change in your position, at least for the next hours to come. Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I abide by what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- it's -- I take it that that's -- you instructed him to -- to tell this. Mr. Kabashi, I couldn't say that this concludes your testimony, because that's not exactly the situation we find ourselves in. The -- you have not answered the one question that was put to you. You have indicated that you would not answer any other question as well. That's at present the situation. Therefore, it's of no use to continue the videolink. I'd like to express my gratitude to you, Mr. Tarlow, and at the same time invite you to bring to our attention whatever you'd - in addition to what has already been said - bring to our attention. But I, first of all, would like to express our gratitude for the assistance provided by the United States for the proceedings before this Tribunal. Do I understand that there's nothing you would like to bring to our attention, Mr. Tarlow?

utterances.speaker: MR. TARLOW
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No, Your Honour, I don't -- I don't think there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Davidson, I understand that you are assigned on very short notice. Thank you for your availability. Mr. Karnavas, the same as far as you are concerned. This concludes the videolink. Of course, also we'd like to thank the representative of the Registry for assisting us in conducting this videolink. Mr. Kabashi, what further steps will be is still to be considered by everyone competent to consider it. This concludes the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any procedural matters the parties would like to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the avoidance of doubt, might I ask that the order that the Chamber has made governing the conditions under which there be communication inter parte directly or indirectly with this witness continue. In other words, if there is any intention - I don't know whether there is - for further communications to take place on the part of the Office of the Prosecutor either with Mr. Karnavas or with the witness or with the witness's US lawyer, that those be conducted under the same conditions as those which were conducted during the interval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a joint request? I see it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, anything to -- in response to this request?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I -- I'm -- I'm not quite sure, is Mr. Emmerson proposing that if I speak to Mr. Karnavas, that he, Mr. Troop, and Mr. Guy-Smith should be there and there should be a conference call or -- or the e-mail should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that the communication is -- that the Defence has an opportunity to follow in every respect the communications between you and those counsel assisting Mr. Kabashi at this time. That's the request. Would it be by e-mail, then I take it that you would like to be copied on the e-mail? Would it be in a personal conversation, that you'd be invited for that conversation. And, of course, within the usual limits of courtesy, that is, not to announce that you'd like to have a conversation with Mr. Karnavas at two minutes past 3.00 this night but -- but reasonable notice. Yes, Mr. Re. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Emmerson is presupposing that the contact would be initiated by the Prosecution, as opposed to, say, Mr. Davidson or Mr. Karnavas coming to the Prosecution and saying, "Look, we've got some news. The news is the following." And that's something I have no control over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm presupposing nothing. We're in a situation where, for whatever extraordinary set of reasons, there is a line of communication open between the Prosecution and a witness who's been sworn. And so whatever mechanism takes place for that communication to be furthered, it will not take place in the manner which is ex parte but inter-parte, as far as the witness is currently -- has been sworn.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He has a lawyer. I wouldn't -- wouldn't go near the witness. I mean, I don't know what Mr. Emmerson is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. -- Mr. -- let me be quite frank, Mr. Re. You were quite near to the witness when you explained to him about arrest warrants, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no intention of attempting to communicate with the witness. I don't have any intention of attempting to communicate with Mr. Davidson either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- okay. Now -- now --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Davidson would approach you and give a message, would you then please invite him to put this message on the e-mail and copy it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And not engage in any conversations of ... Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. May I be clear. I wasn't suggesting that Mr. Re would at this stage take the initiative to contact the witness directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But the whole purpose of this dialogue is to get a message between the Prosecution and the witness via his lawyers. That's the function of the discussions that Mr. Re has been seeking to promote and that's why I say they should take place inter-parte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karnavas, do you have any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I followed the -- the exchange. And I -- I'm fully aware of my obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, rather than an order, could I just make an undertaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the undertaking would be the following. If there's any communication in relation to -- with Mr. Karnavas or Mr. Davidson, I will make sure the Defence are present, if it's personal communication. And if there's any written communication, I'll make sure that it is copied to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that ...? Looking at the Defence, that's -- that's a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Obviously, I assume personal communication would include telephonic communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's understood. Then at the same time, if there would be any exceptional circumstances which would require different matters, a different approach, if the witness would inform Mr. Karnavas that his mother is -- I don't know whether she's still alive -- is about to die and that she would like -- he would like to visit his mother and that he would like to discuss with Mr. Re issues as arrest warrants, that's, of course, issues of a totally different nature. The Chamber would have to be fully informed to grant any exception in that respect. And I gave the example as a rather dramatic example. And that's exactly how it is intended. That is, therefore, to say that any deviation needs the permission of the Chamber and the Chamber should be fully informed about circumstances under which it is asked. Then any other matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There -- there was an issue of -- which is not directly related to what we are doing today. And I'm especially addressing you, Mr. Karnavas. That is, how to communicate filings in a contempt case against Mr. Kabashi with him. The Chamber would rather not rush into this matter at this very moment. It seems to be a technical matter. And with your assistance, it will not be a lot of work. But if your assistance and the assistance of Mr. Davidson could be sought in order to make sure that the usual communication with an accused of -- which is not clear yet whether he will be self-represented or not, to -- how to establish that. We'll deal with that, but not at this moment, not in the context of this case. Then if there's nothing else, then we'll adjourn. The Chamber is inclined to say that we'll resume on Monday, the 26th of November at quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom I, but that, of course, is still dependent on a -- an application to hear Witness 30 at that day. We have granted leave to hear the witness on that day. Of course, it still depends on whether the Prosecution would call the witness for that day. Another matter is that the Chamber has dealt with quite a lot of procedural matters today. Nevertheless, being so close to the conclusion of the Prosecutor's case, the Chamber would -- does not envisage at this moment to have any housekeeping session later this week. At the same time, we cannot exclude that we would need one. Of course, if that would be the case, the Chamber would immediately communicate this to the parties. And again, at this moment, the Chamber doesn't see any reason to schedule it, but as I said earlier, the situation sometimes changes within 50 minutes or within 5 minutes. The Chamber, of course, hopes that this situation will not change for the coming days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, perhaps a -- a final question. As far as the 26th and the -- and the 27th are concerned, have all the practical arrangements been prepared? Could you give us any information about whether it's technically possible at all to hear Witness 30 on the 26th, which, of course, would allow you to make an oral application, if you would wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could Your Honour excuse me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you activate your microphone. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We make the oral application, as I understand it, with the Canadian authorities, the only outstanding issue is whether the Court would allow us to sit on that day. The Canadians have said if the Court allows us -- allows the Prosecution to call the witness on those days, the arrangements will be made. And as I understand it, they're fairly confident the witness will testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's not speculate yet on that, Mr. Re, but the Court has allowed you to call the witness on the 26th, so you now make an oral application to hear the witness on that day in the full confidence that the authorities will take care that the videolink will be established and that all the arrangements are made. Then with the proviso I just made for housekeeping matters, if there will not be any housekeeping session, we adjourn until Monday, the 26th of November, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I.
